title: Janus looks both ways
hook: the Romans named January for Janus, who looks backward and forward

segments.voice: Yesterday: a new year, and Seneca's first letter. Your line was begin now. Did the small first step happen, or is it still waiting on the calendar? Day six hundred sixty-six.

Stand in a doorway for a moment. Behind you, the room you're leaving. In front, the room you're walking into. For a second you're in neither, and you can see both. Ancient Romans gave that spot its own god. His name was Janus, and on coins and statues he has two faces, one looking back and one looking forward. The doorway, the gate, the first hour of the day and the first day of the year all belonged to him. Our word January still carries his name.
screen: `STANDING IN A DOORWAY.` → `TWO FACES, BACK AND FORWARD.` → `JANUARY: JANUS'S MONTH.`

segments.voice: First, who he was to the Romans. Janus was the god of beginnings and passages: doors, gates, the start of things. In Roman worship his name was often called first in prayers, before other gods, because he stood at the opening. The poet Ovid, in his poem on the Roman calendar, has Janus explain his two faces like a doorkeeper who watches both the street and the house. Second, a famous door. In Rome, the gates of a small shrine to Janus were open in wartime and closed in peace. They were rarely closed. The emperor Augustus boasted that they'd been shut three times in his rule. Third, what a Stoic would make of the two faces. Seneca and Marcus both warned about living in the past or the future. Seneca observes that fear and hope march together, and both come from a mind that leans ahead instead of standing in the present. Marcus reminds himself that the only life anyone loses is the moment they're living now. So a Stoic might look at Janus and say: look both ways, yes, but don't move into either room. Fourth, how to look well. Look back to learn, not to replay. What went right? What would you do differently? Look forward to prepare, not to worry. What is one thing to do next? Then step through the doorway into the room that's real, which is this one. Janus himself stands in the threshold, after all, not in the past or the future.
screen: `JANUS: GOD OF DOORS AND BEGINNINGS.` · `GATES SHUT ONLY IN PEACETIME.` · `DON'T MOVE INTO EITHER ROOM.` · `BACK TO LEARN, AHEAD TO PREPARE.` · then, large: `BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand in a real doorway. If not, picture one. Look back first: think of the last few months. Find one thing you learned, just one, and let it be enough. Now turn and look forward: the next few months. Find one thing you want to do, small and clear. Then come back to the doorway itself. Feel your feet. This is the threshold, the only place you ever actually stand. The bell holds the time.
Janus looks both ways: the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, with one face to the past and one to the future, who gave January its name. Today's word.
Your line: both ways. Next time you pass through a door today, glance back once to learn, forward once to prepare, and then walk on. Day six hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Some people mark a new year or a transition by deliberately looking back at what they learned and forward to one clear step, then returning attention to the present.

fork.setup: you're at the threshold of a new year. how would a Stoic use Janus's two faces?
options: replay every mistake of the past year
look back to learn, forward to prepare, then live today
plan every detail of the coming year
fork.reveal: the past and future are for learning and preparing; the life you actually have is the present moment.

original.note: Latin: January, the month of Janus.

trapdoor: what you thought: Janus is a two-faced god, like a two-faced person.
what it means: his two faces watch the past and the future from the doorway, the place of beginnings.
what a scholar hears: ianua is Latin for door; Janus's gates were closed in peace, and Augustus's Res Gestae 13 says they were shut three times under him.

notes: Janus invoked first in Roman prayers (e.g. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2.67; Macrobius): confirm the generalization 'often called first'.
Ovid Fasti 1: Janus compares himself to a doorkeeper watching inside and out. Confirm line range.
Res Gestae 13: the gates of Janus Quirinus closed three times while Augustus was princeps. Confirm.
Letters 5.7–8: Seneca cites Hecato, cease to hope and you will cease to fear; hope and fear march together, from looking ahead. Paraphrased.
Meditations 2.14: one loses only the present moment. Paraphrased.
January named for Janus: the standard etymology; a minority of ancient sources offer alternatives. Kept simple.
'Two-faced person' in the trapdoor refers to the English idiom only, not to anyone's beliefs.
